analysis.one_liner: Eliminates all campaign contribution limits, legalizes corporate and union donations, and ends public financing of presidential campaigns.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 16 Republican cosponsors but never got a hearing, markup, or vote in either committee it was sent to before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out every dollar limit on campaign contributions to federal candidates starting in 2007, and would repeal the century-old ban on direct campaign contributions by corporations and labor unions. It would shut down taxpayer-financed presidential campaigns, including the income tax checkoff that funds them. In exchange, it would tighten disclosure: all campaign reports filed electronically and posted online, every contribution reported within 24 hours in the final 90 days before an election, and stricter accuracy requirements for identifying donors who give more than $200.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy individuals and large corporations, who could legally give unlimited money directly to federal candidates. Incumbent members of Congress, who would gain an unrestricted fundraising edge over challengers. Labor unions would also gain the same legal right to contribute directly.

how_it_helps.text: Removes all limits on how much anyone may contribute to a federal candidate for elections after 2006 [S2][S3].
Repeals the ban on corporations and labor unions making contributions and expenditures in federal elections for elections after December 2006 [S2][S3].

Ends taxpayer financing of presidential campaigns after 2006, terminates the income tax checkoff for the Presidential Election Campaign Fund, and transfers any leftover money to the Treasury's general fund [S2][S3].

Requires electronic filing of all campaign reports and posting them on the Internet, 24-hour reporting of any contribution in the last 90 days before an election, copies of state and local party disbursement reports filed with the FEC, and strict accuracy for identifying donors giving over $200 a year [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Voters without wealth. With no contribution limits and legal corporate money, campaigns would be funded by a small pool of very large donors, giving them far more access and influence over elected officials than ordinary constituents have. Small donors and the public financing system that let average taxpayers support presidential candidates would lose their role.

drawbacks.text: The bill's core is the removal of every contribution cap and the legalization of direct corporate and union campaign money, which would let a single company or billionaire give unlimited sums to a candidate [S2][S3].

The bill's findings argue that limits hurt challengers, but unlimited money tends to favor whoever can raise the most — usually well-connected incumbents and corporate-backed candidates — so its promised level playing field for challengers is highly doubtful [S3].
Taxpayers would lose the voluntary checkoff that funds public financing of presidential campaigns, removing the one system designed to let candidates run without relying on large donors [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency provisions are genuinely useful — electronic filing, 24-hour reporting, and strict donor identification would make it much easier to see where campaign money comes from. But they are the side dish. The main course is unlimited contributions and direct corporate money in federal campaigns, which would concentrate political influence in the hands of the biggest donors. The disclosure improvements do not offset that, because voters would know exactly which large donors bought access while having no way to counteract it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2006 and sent to two committees, House Administration and Ways and Means, and neither one ever acted on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 15, 2006 by Rep. John Doolittle of California, joined by Reps. Herger, Sam Johnson of Texas, and McKeon as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred on the day of introduction to the Committee on House Administration and to the Committee on Ways and Means, whose jurisdiction covered the bill's tax provisions [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the committees reported nothing and the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary voters lost nothing, because the bill never moved: contribution limits, the corporate money ban, and presidential public financing all stayed in place. Voters also did not get the bill's faster electronic disclosure, a modest loss.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill sat untouched in committees controlled by the Republican majority, so no Democrat ever supported it and no committee action ever occurred [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would remove every cap on what any individual could give a federal candidate, letting a single donor hand a campaign an unlimited sum. Public disclosure of those gifts would be instant, but so would the access the money buys.

The bill repeals the ban on direct corporate contributions and expenditures in federal elections, the restriction dating back to 1907. Companies could then fund candidates directly rather than working around limits through separate channels.

Unions would get the same right as corporations to contribute directly to federal candidates. Union political spending is directed at candidates aligned with worker interests, but unlimited sums from any large organization raise the same access concerns.

Unlimited contributions would give sitting members an even larger fundraising edge over challengers, despite the bill's stated goal of helping challengers. The bill died without a vote, so incumbents' current fundraising rules were untouched.

industries.industry: Campaign finance software and compliance vendors
industries.note: The bill would require all campaigns to file reports electronically and post them online, a mandate that would have expanded the market for compliance and filing technology.

industries.industry: Presidential public financing system and its small-dollar contributors
industries.note: The checkoff that lets taxpayers voluntarily fund presidential campaigns would be terminated, and the fund's remaining money swept into the Treasury. Candidates who choose public funds to avoid dependence on big donors would lose that option.
